profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mixed-use industrial park that operates a mature Total Site energy system. The park is considering a strategic expansion over the next 18 months: adding a small gas turbine with heat recovery and connecting a new food-processing unit to the site's shared steam and hot-water network. The meeting is between the site energy lead and the expansion project planner to agree how they will structure the Total Site methodology study, what cases will be evaluated, who will prepare which inputs, and what will be delivered for the executive steering review in three weeks. The agenda is to define the planning study boundary, align on which expansion options are included in the first pass, decide what baseline and utility assumptions will be used, and split responsibilities for data collection and scenario modeling. The expected outcome is an agreed work plan for a strategic Total Site assessment that can inform whether the expansion should proceed as a utility-only integration, a broader process integration, or a staged combination of both.

members.name: Elena Varga
members.expertise: Pinch analysis, utility system optimization, steam and heat recovery network assessment
members.background: Elena is a chemical engineer who has spent eight years improving heat recovery across refinery and district-energy style sites, and she now maintains the site's Total Site models and utility balance assumptions.
members.private_state: Elena wants the planning exercise to stay analytically tractable and comparable to prior Total Site studies so that she can produce a defensible recommendation quickly; she is also concerned that expansion teams often underestimate the disruption caused by changing process connections rather than only utility assets.
hidden_assumptions: If the team says they will start with the 'base case', that means the currently validated Total Site model from last autumn's steam audit, excluding temporary winter operating measures.
If a new unit is 'included in the Total Site', its process heating and cooling loads will be represented in the site profiles, not merely its demand on the existing headers.
A 'first-pass strategic study' should use normalized, representative operating conditions rather than month-specific peak behavior.
When they say the gas turbine option will be 'integrated first', she assumes this means a utility-only change that leaves existing Total Site Profiles unchanged in the initial comparison.

members.name: Marcus Hale
members.expertise: Capital project planning, phased site expansion, stakeholder coordination across industrial and commercial tenants
members.background: Marcus comes from infrastructure development and has led several brownfield expansion programs where utility tie-ins had to be justified early using partial design information.
members.private_state: Marcus wants a planning package that is immediately usable for the steering committee and favors framing the expansion as low-risk and phaseable; he is worried that a broader modeling scope will slow approvals or reveal integration dependencies the sponsors are not ready to fund.
hidden_assumptions: If the team says 'base case', that means the operating configuration currently being used by site management this quarter, including seasonal rented boilers and temporary dispatch practices because those reflect real decision conditions.
If a new unit is 'included in the Total Site', that can mean connected to the shared utility system for planning purposes even if detailed process-level thermal profiles are not yet modeled.
A 'first-pass strategic study' should reflect realistic worst-week capacity pressure so executives can judge whether expansion is safe without utility bottlenecks.

When they say the gas turbine option will be 'integrated first', he assumes this means it is the first project phase and that downstream process integration assumptions can be bundled into the same storyline if they help the business case.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the base case
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using 'the base case' for comparison
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the validated annualized Total Site model from the autumn energy audit, with temporary winter boilers and abnormal dispatch removed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the current quarter's live operating setup, including two rented package boilers and winter-biased utility loading because that is what management sees as today's baseline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe 'base case' is an obvious shared reference because each works from a commonly circulated site pack; neither expects the other to distinguish between the validated analytical baseline and the currently operated seasonal configuration unless the discussion becomes highly technical.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of including the new food-processing unit in the Total Site
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'include the new unit in the Total Site model'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means building process-level thermal representations so the new unit changes the Total Site Profiles and can be assessed with the plus/minus principle as a process integration case.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means representing the unit as an added steam and hot-water consumer connected to the utility network, without requiring full process profile reconstruction in the first planning round.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standard and cooperative in both engineering and project contexts; because each interpretation still involves the unit being 'in the model,' the gap hides behind apparently aligned planning language.

misalignment_points.topic: What first-pass planning conditions should represent
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the first pass should show whether the expansion is 'feasible' and 'robust'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes feasibility is established if the integrated concept improves or at least preserves heat recovery under representative operating conditions and respects acceptable return temperatures in the modeled average case.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes feasibility is established if the site can absorb the expansion during the highest-demand operating week without visible utility shortfalls or extra unplanned rental equipment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Feasibility and robustness are broad approval words used routinely in planning meetings; both assume the other shares their standard of evidence because neither sees their criterion as controversial enough to spell out.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of integrating the gas turbine first
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'look at the gas turbine first' and then the broader extension
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the initial study step isolates a utility-only modification: add the gas turbine and heat recovery loop while holding existing process profiles fixed, then separately test process additions afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes 'gas turbine first' refers to the headline project phase, but the first study package can already incorporate expected process-side changes from the food unit if that strengthens the strategic narrative.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a harmless sequencing shortcut, and both parties favor phased planning; the difference lies in whether 'first' constrains analytical scope or merely presentation order, which feels too second-order to state explicitly.

If we compare the expansion options consistently against that, I can show a clear integration route without reopening every operating exception.
